What you will learn

  1. A cosine-based change score between two years of the same point's embedding
  2. Why a fixed change-score threshold is not itself a semantic-change decision
  3. Calibrating a threshold against an independent reference with precision_recall_curve
  4. Per-year classifiers and a land-cover transition matrix (second half of this notebook, authored in a later plan)
Prerequisite Needed?
Python, NumPy/pandas basics Yes
Earth Engine account No
GIS background No

Time to complete: ~3 minutes execution. Runs on free Colab CPU, no Earth Engine account.

Course reference environment: 2026-08 release. Provider APIs may change. Every cloud notebook has a local/offline fallback.

Data: 2018 vs 2021, row-aligned by sample_id

This module compares 2018 against 2021 rather than 2020 against 2024: Copernicus imperviousness has a series break between its 2015 and 2018 products, and the corresponding change product covers 2018-2021. The frozen tables carry 2018, 2021 and 2024 for the same sample_ids across both study areas, so a 2018/2021 pair joins directly without any extra sampling.

blocks.code:
aligned = {}
for area in ("bern", "seville"):
    gdf_early = loaded[(area, years[0])].set_index("sample_id")
    gdf_late = loaded[(area, years[1])].set_index("sample_id")
    shared_ids = gdf_early.index.intersection(gdf_late.index)
    assert len(shared_ids) == len(gdf_early) == len(gdf_late), (
        f"{area}: expected an exact sample_id match between {years[0]} and "
        f"{years[1]} (frozen tables share sample_id across years per "
        f"data/DATA_CARD.md), got {len(shared_ids)} shared out of "
        f"{len(gdf_early)}/{len(gdf_late)} rows -- a partial join here would "
        "silently compare unrelated points."
    )
    aligned[area] = {
        years[0]: gdf_early.loc[shared_ids].reset_index(),
        years[1]: gdf_late.loc[shared_ids].reset_index(),
    }
    print(f"{area}: {len(shared_ids)} row-aligned points ({years[0]} vs {years[1]})")

blocks.html: Takeaway: the same sample_id names the same real-world point across 2018 and 2021 -- that stability is what makes a paired change score meaningful. Without it, subtracting one year's embedding from another would be comparing unrelated pixels, and the resulting "change score" would be noise dressed up as a measurement.

Change score: 1 - cosine_similarity per point

course.embeddings.change_score takes two row-aligned (n, 64) matrices and returns one (n,) array: how far each point's embedding moved between the two years, as a single number. It reports representation movement only -- it does not know, and does not claim to know, why a point moved.

blocks.code:
from course.embeddings import change_score

frames = []
for area in ("bern", "seville"):
    gdf_early = aligned[area][years[0]]
    gdf_late = aligned[area][years[1]]
    matrix_early = course.schema.to_matrix(gdf_early)
    matrix_late = course.schema.to_matrix(gdf_late)
    scores = change_score(matrix_early, matrix_late)
    frames.append(
        pd.DataFrame(
            {
                "sample_id": gdf_late["sample_id"],
                "region": area,
                "lon": gdf_late["lon"],
                "lat": gdf_late["lat"],
                "change_score": scores,
                "imd_2018": gdf_late["imd_2018"],
                "label": gdf_late["label"],
            }
        )
    )
change_df = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)
print(change_df.groupby("region")["change_score"].describe())

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4), sharey=True)
for ax, area in zip(axes, ("bern", "seville")):
    ax.hist(change_df.loc[change_df["region"] == area, "change_score"], bins=50)
    ax.set_title(area)
    ax.set_xlabel("change score (1 - cosine similarity)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("count")
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("figures/03_change_score_hist.png")
plt.show()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))
for ax, area in zip(axes, ("bern", "seville")):
    sub = change_df.loc[change_df["region"] == area]
    sc = ax.scatter(sub["lon"], sub["lat"], c=sub["change_score"], s=8, cmap="viridis")
    ax.set_title(area)
    ax.set_xlabel("lon")
fig.colorbar(sc, ax=axes, label="change score", shrink=0.8)
axes[0].set_ylabel("lat")
fig.savefig("figures/03_change_score_map.png")
plt.show()

blocks.html:
The WRONG conclusion

It is tempting to pick a threshold by eye and call every point above it "artificialized." The cell below does exactly that -- and it is wrong.

blocks.why_html:
Why this is wrong

1 - cosine_similarity collapses the full 64-dimensional embedding into one number, and 0.25 was picked by eye with no reference data behind it. Google's own analysis of change scores derived this way found "widespread speckling, scattered false positives" -- harvest cycles, a drought year, early snow cover, or a swath-boundary artifact in the underlying imagery can all move a point's embedding by as much as genuine land-cover change does. A large change score means the representation moved; it does not by itself mean the land cover changed, let alone that it became "artificialized" specifically. Treating an unvalidated cutoff as a semantic-change decision is Pitfall 5 of this course, and it is the reason the rest of this section calibrates a threshold against a reference instead of asserting one.

output.text: WRONG: bern=121 of 2050 points flagged, seville=148 of 2050 points flagged

blocks.html:
Calibrating a threshold against a proxy independent reference

The true Copernicus HRL Imperviousness Change 2018-2021 product would be the right reference here -- but it requires a free EU Login the author has not created for this course (see 02-RESEARCH.md, "Is the free EU Login genuinely needed?"). Rather than skip validation, or worse, quietly reuse label as if it were an independent change product, this notebook builds an explicitly labeled proxy from two columns already in the frozen tables:

  • known_change: imd_2018 < 20 (measurably non-impervious in 2018) and label == "built" (labeled built by the 2021-sourced WorldCover pass).
  • known_unchanged: either stayed built (imd_2018 >= 70 and label == "built"), or stayed clearly non-built (imd_2018 < 20 and label != "built").

This proxy is weaker than a real two-epoch change product for a specific reason: label is a single 2021 snapshot, not a genuine 2018-vs-2021 label pair, so "known_change" here really means "was clearly non-built in 2018 and is built in the one epoch we have a label for" -- consistent with a 2018-2021 transition to built, but not directly observed as one. A student with an EU Login should replace this proxy with the true HRL change product and re-run this calibration; what follows is the honest, currently-available substitute, not a claim of equivalence.

blocks.code:
known_change = (change_df["imd_2018"] < 20) & (change_df["label"] == "built")
known_unchanged = ((change_df["imd_2018"] >= 70) & (change_df["label"] == "built")) | (
    (change_df["imd_2018"] < 20) & (change_df["label"] != "built")
)
controls = change_df.loc[known_change | known_unchanged].copy()
controls["y_true"] = known_change.loc[controls.index].astype(int)
print(
    f"controls: {len(controls)}/{len(change_df)} rows kept "
    f"({int(known_change.sum())} known_change, {int(known_unchanged.sum())} known_unchanged)"
)

from sklearn.metrics import f1_score, precision_score, recall_score
from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve

precision_curve, recall_curve, thresholds = precision_recall_curve(
    controls["y_true"], controls["change_score"]
)
f1_curve = np.where(
    (precision_curve[:-1] + recall_curve[:-1]) > 0,
    2 * precision_curve[:-1] * recall_curve[:-1]
    / (precision_curve[:-1] + recall_curve[:-1] + 1e-9),
    0.0,
)
best_idx = int(np.argmax(f1_curve))
best_threshold = float(thresholds[best_idx])
print(f"calibrated threshold (max F1 on controls): {best_threshold:.3f}")

calibrated_pred = (controls["change_score"] > best_threshold).astype(int)
precision = precision_score(controls["y_true"], calibrated_pred)
recall = recall_score(controls["y_true"], calibrated_pred)
f1 = f1_score(controls["y_true"], calibrated_pred)
print(f"overall: precision={precision:.3f}, recall={recall:.3f}, f1={f1:.3f}")

for group_name, mask in [
    ("known_change controls", controls["y_true"] == 1),
    ("known_unchanged controls", controls["y_true"] == 0),
]:
    group = controls.loc[mask]
    group_pred = (group["change_score"] > best_threshold).astype(int)
    flagged_rate = group_pred.mean()
    print(f"{group_name}: {len(group)} points, flagged rate={flagged_rate:.2f}")

blocks.html:
Takeaway: the calibrated threshold above is not just "a different number" than 0.25 -- it comes with a precision, a recall, and an F1 score measured against a labeled reference, so you know how much to trust a flag it produces. The 0.25 threshold from the WRONG-conclusion cell came with none of that. The proxy reference used here is honestly weaker than the true HRL 2018-2021 change product would be (it leans on a single 2021 label snapshot, not a genuine two-epoch label), and this notebook says so explicitly rather than presenting it as equivalent -- a student with an EU Login should swap in the real change product and recalibrate.

What's next: the rest of this notebook adds per-year classifiers and a land-cover transition matrix on top of this same change-score foundation, then validates both approaches with spatially- and temporally-grouped cross-validation.

Per-year classifiers and a class-transition matrix

The change score above answers "how far did the embedding move," but it cannot answer "moved from what to what." A transition matrix can: fit one classifier per year on that year's own embeddings, predict every point's class in each year, and cross-tabulate the two predictions.

Important caveat, stated before the code below runs it: label does not itself vary by year -- WorldCover 2021 is the only labeled epoch in this dataset. So "per-year classifier" here does NOT mean "trained against a year-specific ground truth." It means: train the identical model architecture separately on each year's own embedding distribution (still supervised by the same 2021 label column, pooled across both regions), then predict from each year's embeddings. The interesting signal is where clf_2018's prediction and clf_2021's prediction disagree for the same point -- something a single continuous change score cannot show, because it never assigns a class at all.

blocks.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

CLASSES = ["built", "crop", "vegetation", "water"]

pooled = {}
for year in years:
    frames_year = []
    for area in ("bern", "seville"):
        gdf_year = aligned[area][year]
        frames_year.append(gdf_year.loc[gdf_year["label"].isin(CLASSES)])
    pooled[year] = pd.concat(frames_year, ignore_index=True)
    print(f"{year}: {len(pooled[year])} pooled rows after dropping 'bare'")

classifiers = {}
predictions = {}
for year in years:
    X_year = course.schema.to_matrix(pooled[year])
    y_year = pooled[year]["label"].to_numpy()
    clf = Pipeline(
        [
            ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
            ("clf", LogisticRegression(random_state=RANDOM_STATE, max_iter=1000)),
        ]
    )
    clf.fit(X_year, y_year)
    classifiers[year] = clf
    predictions[year] = clf.predict(X_year)
    print(f"{year}: classifier fit on {len(y_year)} pooled points")

blocks.html: The two pooled tables are already row-aligned by sample_id within each area (the aligned dict built earlier), and pooled[2018]/pooled[2021] were built with the identical per-area concatenation order and the identical bare-dropping filter, so predictions[2018][i] and predictions[2021][i] refer to the same real-world point.

from sklearn.metrics import ConfusionMatrixDisplay, confusion_matrix

pred_2018 = predictions[years[0]]
pred_2021 = predictions[years[1]]

transition = confusion_matrix(pred_2018, pred_2021, labels=CLASSES)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6))
ConfusionMatrixDisplay(transition, display_labels=CLASSES).plot(ax=ax, colorbar=False)
ax.set_xlabel("predicted 2021 class")
ax.set_ylabel("predicted 2018 class")
ax.set_title("Class-transition matrix (predicted, not true, classes)")
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("figures/03_transition_matrix.png")
plt.show()

blocks.html: Why the axis labels say "predicted," never "true": every cell in this matrix comes from two classifier predictions, not from any 2018-vs-2021 ground-truth transition label (none exists in this dataset). Reading it as observed truth would silently overstate how much is actually validated here.

blocks.html:
Comparing the transition-matrix mask against the continuous change score

pooled[years[1]] drops the bare class that change_df still carries, so the two tables cannot be compared by row position -- join on sample_id (unique per point within a region, matched together with region since both regions reuse the same sample_id numbering).

blocks.code:
mask_lookup = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "sample_id": pooled[years[1]]["sample_id"],
        "region": pooled[years[1]]["region"],
        "artificialized_mask": artificialized_mask,
    }
)
joined = change_df.merge(mask_lookup, on=["sample_id", "region"], how="inner")
assert len(joined) == len(mask_lookup), (
    f"expected every classifier-pooled point ({len(mask_lookup)}) to also "
    f"appear in change_df, got {len(joined)} matched rows -- a join key "
    "mismatch would silently drop points from this comparison"
)

joined["cosine_wrong"] = joined["change_score"] > 0.25
joined["cosine_calibrated"] = joined["change_score"] > best_threshold

comparison_rows = []
for name, col in [
    ("WRONG threshold (0.25)", "cosine_wrong"),
    ("calibrated threshold", "cosine_calibrated"),
]:
    mask_col = joined["artificialized_mask"]
    cosine_col = joined[col]
    both = int((mask_col & cosine_col).sum())
    mask_only = int((mask_col & ~cosine_col).sum())
    cosine_only = int((~mask_col & cosine_col).sum())
    comparison_rows.append(
        {
            "cosine flag": name,
            "transition-mask only": mask_only,
            "cosine only": cosine_only,
            "both": both,
        }
    )
disagreement_table = pd.DataFrame(comparison_rows)
print(disagreement_table)

blocks.html: Takeaway: the transition-matrix mask and the continuous change score answer different questions -- cosine measures how far the embedding vector moved, the transition matrix asks what class it moved between. They only partly agree, and that disagreement is itself the teaching point (Pitfall 5): a point can move a lot in embedding space without crossing the vegetation-to-built class boundary (phenology, a dry year), and a point can cross that boundary with a modest cosine movement if the two classes' embedding centroids are already close. Neither number alone tells the whole story; that is exactly why this notebook builds both.

Validating the artificialization mask: spatially- and temporally-grouped CV

artificialized_mask above is itself the output of a classifier (well, two). Before trusting it, this notebook validates it the same honest way Module 3 validated the land-cover classifier -- with grouped CV, never a random split.

A second trap lurks here that Module 3 did not have: temporal leakage. The pooled 2018+2021 table contains the SAME real-world locations twice (once per year). A random split -- or even a spatial split that ignores year -- can put a point's 2018 row in the training fold and its 2021 row in the test fold. The model would then partly "recognise the site" (soil colour, terrain, whatever is stable across both years) rather than learn a signal that transfers to genuinely new locations or new years. This is the temporal analogue of Module 3's spatial-block lesson: group by the thing that must NOT leak across the split, spatial blocks there, year here.

blocks.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, LeaveOneGroupOut

from course.config import BLOCK_SIZE_M
from course.validation import make_blocks, spatial_cv_report

pooled_all = pd.concat([pooled[years[0]], pooled[years[1]]], ignore_index=True)
mask_all = np.concatenate([artificialized_mask, artificialized_mask])
year_array = np.concatenate(
    [
        np.full(len(pooled[years[0]]), years[0]),
        np.full(len(pooled[years[1]]), years[1]),
    ]
)
X_pooled_all = course.schema.to_matrix(pooled_all)

pooled_2056 = pooled_all.to_crs("EPSG:2056")
spatial_blocks = make_blocks(pooled_2056, block_size_m=BLOCK_SIZE_M)
n_blocks = len(np.unique(spatial_blocks))
print(f"pooled table: {n_blocks} spatial blocks at {BLOCK_SIZE_M} m")

artif_model = Pipeline(
    [
        ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
        ("clf", LogisticRegression(random_state=RANDOM_STATE, max_iter=1000)),
    ]
)

spatial_report = spatial_cv_report(
    artif_model,
    X_pooled_all,
    mask_all,
    groups=spatial_blocks,
    cv=GroupKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
)
print(
    f"SPATIAL-BLOCK CV: balanced_accuracy="
    f"{spatial_report['mean_balanced_accuracy']:.3f} ± "
    f"{spatial_report['std_balanced_accuracy']:.3f}"
)

blocks.html: Takeaway: the numbers printed above are the honest, measured comparison -- not an assumed direction. If leave-one-year-out scores lower than spatial-block CV, that supports the hypothesis this section opened with: year-specific artifacts (Sentinel swath differences, atmospheric conditions, a different phenological state) make the model partly overfit to a year's own signature rather than learn a transferable artificialization signal, and spatial-block CV alone would have hidden that gap because it never separates by year. If the two scores land close together instead, that is reported just as plainly: it would mean this mask generalizes across years about as well as it generalizes across space, on this sample. Either way, grouping by the dimension that must not leak -- space for the spatial split, year for this one -- is what makes the number trustworthy in the first place.

blocks.html:
Wrap-up

Takeaways:

  • A cosine-based change score reports how far a point's embedding moved between two years -- a real, cheap signal, but not by itself a semantic change decision. Calibrating a threshold against an independent proxy reference (precision_recall_curve) turns it into one with a known precision/recall/F1, unlike an eyeballed cutoff.
  • A class-transition matrix built from two per-year classifiers answers a different, more direct question: what class did a point move from and to? The two approaches agree only partly -- that disagreement, not either number alone, is the honest picture of what changed.
  • Both the calibrated change-score threshold and this transition-matrix artificialization mask stay honest about a real limitation: the true Copernicus HRL Imperviousness change product (2018-2021) requires a free EU Login the author has not created for this course, so this notebook validates against the best available proxy and says so, rather than presenting the proxy as equivalent to a real change product.
  • Validating the artificialization mask required grouping by TWO different things that must not leak across a CV split: space (the Module 3 lesson, reused here via make_blocks/GroupKFold) and year (this module's new lesson, via LeaveOneGroupOut grouped on the year label) -- label_source (esa_worldcover_2021) and validation_source (eea_hrl_imperviousness_2018) also stay two architecturally distinct strings throughout, never conflated (Pitfall 6).

What's next: Module 5 reuses these SAME course.embeddings.change_score and course.validation.spatial_cv_report helpers across TESSERA, Clay and LGND embeddings, so the change-detection and validation logic built here stays identical across providers.

    • Copernicus HRL Imperviousness Density 2018 -- Free/open, commercial use allowed -- "Generated using European Union's Copernicus Land Monitoring Service information"
  • Limitation repeated once more for anyone skimming only this section: the true HRL Imperviousness Change 2018-2021 product needs a free EU Login the author has not created for this course; both correction paths above (calibrated threshold, transition-matrix mask) validate against the best currently-available proxy, not that product.

quiz.prompt_html: In the notebook, change_score > 0.25 is used to flag points as "artificialized." What is wrong with this specific threshold?

options.label: A
options.text: 0.25 is too low a value; it should be closer to 1.0.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** The cell is explicitly tagged wrong-conclusion and headed "The WRONG conclusion" — the problem is not the numeric value chosen, it is that any unvalidated cutoff picked by eye is being treated as a semantic-change decision. Raising the number would not fix that.

options.label: B
options.text:
A fixed, eyeballed threshold has no precision/recall/F1 behind it,
so a large change score means the *representation* moved, not that
the *land cover* changed.
options.explanation_html: Correct.** The "Why this is wrong" section states directly: "A large change score means the representation moved; it does not by itself mean the land cover changed, let alone that it became 'artificialized' specifically. Treating an unvalidated cutoff as a semantic-change decision is Pitfall 5 of this course."

options.label: C
options.text:
`1 - cosine_similarity` cannot be computed for embeddings from
different years.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** The notebook computes exactly this ("Change score: 1 - cosine_similarity per point" section) — the computation itself is fine; the trap is in how the number is interpreted afterward.

options.label: D
options.text: The threshold should be calculated separately for Bern and Seville.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** The notebook's fix is calibration against a labeled reference (precision_recall_curve), not regional re-splitting of the same unvalidated eyeball cutoff — see "Calibrating a threshold against a proxy independent reference."

quiz.prompt_html: What does calibrating the threshold with precision_recall_curve on the controls table actually buy you, that the 0.25 cutoff did not have?

options.label: A
options.text:
A threshold with a known precision, recall, and F1 measured against
a labeled reference, so you know how much to trust a flag it produces.
options.explanation_html: Correct.** The Takeaway after the calibration cells states: "the calibrated threshold above is not just 'a different number' than 0.25 -- it comes with a precision, a recall, and an F1 score measured against a labeled reference, so you know how much to trust a flag it produces. The 0.25 threshold ... came with none of that."

options.label: B
options.text:
Proof that the calibrated threshold is the true HRL Imperviousness
Change 2018-2021 product.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** The same section states the proxy "is weaker than a real two-epoch change product" and that "the true Copernicus HRL Imperviousness Change 2018-2021 product would be the right reference here -- but it requires a free EU Login the author has not created."

options.label: C
options.text:
A guarantee that the calibrated threshold will flag fewer points
than 0.25 did.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** The notebook prints both counts side by side ("WRONG threshold ... flagged" vs "calibrated threshold ... flagged") without asserting a direction; which one flags more depends on the run, not on a guarantee.

options.label: D
options.text: A way to avoid needing any independent reference at all.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** Calibration requires the controls table built from known_change/known_unchanged — an independent reference is exactly what makes calibration possible, not what it avoids.

quiz.prompt_html: A point's change score is large. What can you conclude?

options.label: A
options.text:
The point's embedding moved a large distance between the two years
in representation space -- nothing more, without further validation.
options.explanation_html: Correct.** "Why this is wrong" is explicit: cosine "collapses the full 64-dimensional embedding into one number" and reports movement only; per the Module wrap-up Takeaway, "A cosine-based change score reports how far a point's embedding moved between two years -- a real, cheap signal, but not by itself a semantic change decision."

options.label: B
options.text: The land cover at that point definitely changed.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** Same Takeaway: reports of movement are "not by itself a semantic change decision" — the notebook explicitly lists non-change causes ("harvest cycles, a drought year, early snow cover, or a swath-boundary artifact") that can move a score just as much as real change.

options.label: C
options.text: The point was necessarily artificialized (became built).
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** The wrong-conclusion cell is the demonstration of exactly this error — asserting "artificialized" from the raw score alone is the deliberate trap the notebook exists to correct.

options.label: D
options.text: The classifier's prediction for that point is unreliable.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** Change score and classifier confidence are two different, separately-computed signals in this notebook; a large change score says nothing about classifier confidence on its own.

quiz.prompt_html: The notebook validates its calibrated threshold against a "proxy" reference built from imd_2018 and label rather than the true Copernicus HRL Imperviousness Change 2018-2021 product. Why is this proxy explicitly described as weaker than a true two-epoch change product?

options.label: A
options.text:
Because `label` is a single 2021 snapshot, not a genuine
2018-vs-2021 label pair, so "known_change" really means "was clearly
non-built in 2018 and is built in the one epoch we have a label for" —
consistent with a transition, but not directly observed as one.
options.explanation_html: Correct.** Quoted verbatim from "Calibrating a threshold against a proxy independent reference": "This proxy is weaker than a real two-epoch change product for a specific reason: label is a single 2021 snapshot, not a genuine 2018-vs-2021 label pair."

options.label: B
options.text: Because `imd_2018` values are unreliable measurements.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** The notebook never questions imd_2018's measurement quality; the stated weakness is about the label's single-epoch nature, not measurement error.

options.label: C
options.text: Because the proxy only covers the Bern study area.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** known_change/known_unchanged are computed on change_df, which is built from both bern and seville in the "Change score" section above.

options.label: D
options.text:
Because the frozen tables do not contain enough rows to calibrate a
threshold.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** The notebook prints "controls: N/M rows kept" and proceeds with calibration; row count is never cited as the limitation.

quiz.prompt_html: The transition matrix built from clf_2018 and clf_2021 labels its axes "predicted 2018 class" / "predicted 2021 class," never "true." Why does this distinction matter?

options.label: A
options.text:
Because every cell in the matrix comes from two classifier
predictions, not from any 2018-vs-2021 ground-truth transition label —
reading it as observed truth would silently overstate how much is
actually validated.
options.explanation_html: Correct.** Quoted verbatim: "Why the axis labels say 'predicted,' never 'true': every cell in this matrix comes from two classifier predictions, not from any 2018-vs-2021 ground-truth transition label (none exists in this dataset). Reading it as observed truth would silently overstate how much is actually validated here."

options.label: B
options.text: Because the classifiers were trained on unlabeled data.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** Both clf_2018 and clf_2021 are LogisticRegression fit on the pooled 2021 label column — supervised training, just applied to each year's own embedding distribution.

options.label: C
options.text: Because "predicted" and "true" mean the same thing in this context.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** The whole point of the caveat is that they do not mean the same thing here — no 2018-2021 ground-truth transition label exists in this dataset.

options.label: D
options.text:
Because the matplotlib `ConfusionMatrixDisplay` widget cannot render
a "true" axis label.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** This is a labeling/interpretation choice made deliberately in the code, not a plotting-library limitation.

quiz.prompt_html: Why does validating the artificialization mask require grouping by year (LeaveOneGroupOut on year_array) in addition to grouping by spatial block?

options.label: A
options.text:
Because the pooled 2018+2021 table contains the SAME real-world
locations twice, and a split that ignores year could let a point's
2018 row train the model that then predicts its own 2021 row —
"recognising the site" rather than learning a transferable signal.
options.explanation_html: Correct.** Quoted from "Validating the artificialization mask": "The pooled 2018+2021 table contains the SAME real-world locations twice (once per year). A random split -- or even a spatial split that ignores year -- can put a point's 2018 row in the training fold and its 2021 row in the test fold. The model would then partly 'recognise the site' ... rather than learn a signal that transfers."

options.label: B
options.text: Because `GroupKFold` cannot be used with fewer than 10 splits.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** The notebook uses GroupKFold(n_splits=5, ...) for the spatial-block validation; split count is not the reason year-grouping is needed.

options.label: C
options.text: Because 2018 and 2021 use different embedding dimensionalities.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** Both years use the same 64-D AlphaEarth embeddings; X_pooled_all is a single matrix built from both years identically.

options.label: D
options.text:
Because spatial blocks and years are mathematically the same
grouping variable.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** The notebook explicitly treats them as two distinct things that must each independently not leak: "grouping by TWO different things that must not leak across a CV split: space ... and year."

quiz.prompt_html: The notebook reports the calibrated detector's measured precision and F1 against the proxy reference honestly, even when those numbers are weak (e.g., a low precision/F1 rather than a strong one). What is the correct takeaway from a weak measured score here?

options.label: A
options.text:
The weak number invalidates calibration entirely, so the 0.25
eyeballed threshold should be trusted instead.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** The wrap-up Takeaway is unambiguous that the calibrated path, even with a modest score, "comes with a precision, a recall, and an F1 score measured against a labeled reference" while the 0.25 threshold "came with none of that" — a known-weak number is still more trustworthy than an unmeasured one.

options.label: B
options.text:
A weak, honestly-measured score reflects a weak reference (a
single-year label snapshot standing in for a true two-epoch change
product), not necessarily a failure of the calibration method itself.
options.explanation_html: Correct.** This is the notebook's own framing: the proxy "is weaker than a real two-epoch change product" by construction (Q4), so a modest precision/F1 against it is an honest reflection of the proxy's own limits, exactly the point the "proxy" section and its Takeaway make — swap in the true HRL product and recalibrate for a stronger number.

options.label: C
options.text:
A weak score means the change-score computation itself
(`1 - cosine_similarity`) is implemented incorrectly.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** The checkpoint-tagged cells validate the computation elsewhere in the course (e.g., Module 3's unit-norm assertion); a weak precision/F1 here is about reference quality, not arithmetic correctness.

options.label: D
options.text:
Weak calibration numbers should be omitted from the notebook so
students only see favorable results.
options.explanation_html: Incorrect.** The notebook's whole design — printing both threshold counts, both CV scenarios, and stating the proxy's weakness explicitly — is built around reporting honestly measured numbers rather than curating only favorable ones.
